title: How to Really Listen
objective: After this level you can use a simple method to listen closely to any piece of music.
summary: Copland's three planes: sensuous, expressive, sheerly musical. Listen in passes (beat, melody, harmony), and closely rather than loudly: WHO allows 80 dB for 40 hours a week.

cards.headline: Are you just listening, or listening for something?
cards.body: In 1939, the American composer Aaron Copland wrote a book called What to Listen for in Music. His goal was to turn passive listeners into active ones: not someone who is just listening, "but someone who is listening for something." Here is his map, a method built from this tree, and one rule to protect your ears.

items.label: Sensuous
points: The pleasure of the sound itself

items.label: Expressive
points: What the music makes you feel

cards.headline: Listen in three passes
cards.body: Copland noticed that casual listeners catch the melody first, then the rhythm, and take harmony and tone color for granted. So give them turns. Pick one song. First pass: tap the beat (Level 4). Second: hum the melody (Level 5). Third: ignore the tune and follow the chords underneath (Level 6). Copland said we really hear on all three planes at once; the passes just train you to notice.

cards.headline: Listen closely, not loudly
cards.body: WHO says 80 decibels is safe for up to 40 hours a week, but at 90 decibels safe time drops to four hours: ten decibels louder cuts your time to a tenth. It suggests keeping your device at no more than 60% of maximum. Remember Level 10's hair cells, sorting pitch in the cochlea? Human hair cells don't grow back. But noise-induced hearing loss is completely preventable.

mascot.line: Close listening is a quiet sport. Your ears have a lot more music ahead of them.

cards.headline: Listening: sharpened
learned: Copland's planes: sensuous, expressive, sheerly musical
Listen in passes: beat, then melody, then harmony

questions.prompt: In Copland's three planes of listening, what does the sheerly musical plane focus on?

options.label: The notes themselves: melody, rhythm, harmony
The pleasure of the sound alone
The feelings the music gives you

questions.explanation: The sheerly musical plane is the notes themselves and what happens to them: melody, rhythm, harmony and tone color.

questions.prompt: Your music at 80 dB is safe for up to 40 hours a week. Per WHO, what happens if you turn it up to 90 dB?

options.label: Safe time rises to 80 hours
options.rationale: Louder means less safe time, not more.

options.label: Nothing changes
options.rationale: Ten decibels makes a big difference.

options.label: Safe time drops to about 4 hours

questions.explanation: WHO says 90 dB is safe for only about four hours a week: ten decibels louder cuts safe time to a tenth.

questions.prompt: Level 10 showed the cochlea's hair cells sorting pitch. Why does protecting them from loud music matter so much?

options.label: They grow back only during sleep
options.rationale: Human hair cells don't grow back at all.

options.label: Human hair cells don't grow back once lost
Loud music only harms the eardrum
They sort only low pitches anyway
options.rationale: They sort every pitch, high at the wide end.

questions.explanation: Human hair cells don't grow back, so noise-induced hearing loss is permanent, though completely preventable.
